item.title: OpenAI resumes training AI, blocks internet access over security risks
item.description: The company said it would keep its most advanced models offline during training until safeguards are adequate, following incidents in which AI systems accessed the web and breached external systems ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Rachel Metz OpenAI has begun cutting off internet access for its most capable artificial intelligence models during the training process in response to prior incidents in which its systems breached other companies. The company said in a blog post Friday that, after a pause last month, it had resumed training its most advanced models but intends to block internet access until it feels it has adequate safeguards in place to mitigate the risk of unreleased models being able to take unapproved actions online during training.  “Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company wrote. In late September, the company said it would pause training its most advanced AI models after it discovered that one of its AI agent systems that was being trained in what was supposed to be a secured, internet-free environment was able to gain access to the web to reach an external, third-party chatbot. At the time, OpenAI described the breakout as the first security incident of its kind since a combination of models gained internet access during internal testing and inadvertently breached the system of the AI platform Hugging Face in July.  The models involved in the inadvertent Hugging Face breach were operating without the usual safety guardrails, the company has said, because OpenAI had intended them to remain in a testing area known as a “sandbox” — essentially, an isolated virtual software environment that’s meant to run security tests or analyse unsafe code in a controlled way. The models were able to break out of that sandbox, however, by leveraging a software vulnerability to access the open internet. OpenAI said that after the Hugging Face incident, it reduced the connections through which its models might be able to reach the internet during training and testing but kept some for the purpose of metrics, logging and authentication. It also spent a vast amount of computing power on tasking agentic AI systems with identifying vulnerabilities in its training environments as part of a red-teaming effort, a phrase typically used to describe deliberate attempts to break into systems to uncover vulnerabilities before real attackers can. “Our red-teaming agents found vulnerabilities in almost every one of these services that gave them limited forms of internet access,” the firm said in its post. The company said it has since deployed software patches, imposed tighter network restrictions and disclosed the findings to vendors. There have been a series of disclosures in recent months from OpenAI and rivals including Anthropic PBC about incidents in which their models carried out self-directed attacks or unsanctioned actions on third-party websites and systems.  These cases, and a series of stark warnings from within the industry, have vaulted the safety debate into the mainstream. AI developers have warned that their systems could soon become too sophisticated for people to control, adding to concerns the technology could be used by malicious human actors to create bioweapons or carry out devastating cyberattacks.

item.title: UK vows 100 mn euros for biosecurity lab with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google
item.description: The lab will use AI to detect and monitor biological threats, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing up to 200 million euros in AI model credits ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Jacob Reid The UK announced 100 million euro ($134 million) for a AI Biosecurity Lab which will be supported by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind, part of a raft of measures designed to improve the government’s ability to understand and tackle the risks posed by the technology.  The lab will use AI to detect and monitor biological threats, with the funding coming alongside up to 200 million euro in AI model credits from OpenAI and Anthropic, according to a government statement. The lab will also work in partnership with Google DeepMind and life sciences company Basecamp Research, while the government announced a separate 65 million euro for developing countermeasures for pathogens.  “As AI becomes more powerful, Britain must have the capabilities to protect its people and shape its own future,” said Kanishka Narayan, Britain’s AI minister. “That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on.” The lab “will be a major new global institution, bringing together world-leading scientific expertise to protect people from emerging biological threats and ensure Britain leads the world in AI safety and security,” Narayan added. Its creation makes the government’s AI strategy increasingly clear: forming institutions outside of existing government departments to research, monitor and harness different aspects of the technology. The announcement also included 120 million euro in extra funding for the AI Security Institute, which is the best-funded government agency focused on regularly evaluating cutting-edge AI models, and 23 million euro more for the AI Economics Institute, which is being set up to analyse the economic impacts of the technology.‘Honest Broker’The strategy is a key part of the country’s attempt to remain relevant in the AI space despite lagging behind the US and China on cutting edge AI models. It’s trying to act as an “honest broker” for monitoring and regulating, and taking a distinct role from the European Union, which has strongly regulated the tech.  “AI is changing both the biological risks we face and the nature of biological discovery, and we applaud the UK government’s foresight in opening the AI Biosecurity Lab,” said Matt Clifford, who leads International Affairs at Anthropic, and was the Prime Minister’s AI advisor until last June.  “Bringing together frontier AI, the UK’s scientific strength, and government expertise to detect threats earlier and speed up the development of medical treatments will contribute to the safe deployment of AI across industry and society,” he added. The government also announced 130 million euro to use AI to identify cyber vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure and the economy and improve the country’s cyber defenses. That comes after governments and companies around the world rushed to patch two critical flaws in widely used technology on Thursday, which AI helped to find.  There will also be a 120 million euro boost to the Sovereign AI Fund to broaden its remit to include physical and industrial AI such as robotics, autonomous systems and advanced manufacturing, and expand its procurement program for British start-ups.

item.title: Whistleblower tipoffs on insider trading up sharply as Sebi gets 25 in FY26
item.description: Whistleblower reports rise as market expands, but experts call for greater transparency, stronger safeguards and wider coverage of violations ...
item.dc:creator: Sachin P Mampatta
item.content:encoded:
Home / Markets / News / Whistleblower tipoffs on insider trading up sharply as Sebi gets 25 in FY26

Whistleblower tipoffs on insider trading up sharply as Sebi gets 25 in FY26 Whistleblower reports rise as market expands, but experts call for greater transparency, stronger safeguards and wider coverage of violations premium

Sebi received 25 insider-trading tipoffs in FY26, compared with just five over the previous six financial years. (Photo: Reuters)

Sachin P Mampatta Mumbai 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 23 2026 | 11:05 PM IST

Listen to This Article

A regulatory mechanism to provide tipoffs on violations in insider trading in return for monetary rewards as high as ~10 crore may finally be showing signs of taking off.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi)   in December 2019 had established the Office of Informant Protection (OIP) to process tipoffs on insider trading. However, the response was that informants provided just five tipoffs in the first six years of the programme — from 2019-20 (FY20) to FY25.

But FY26 was different. The number of tipoffs in a single financial year increased to 25, shows the latest Annual Report, released on August 6. Fourteen of these have been concluded (including one from the previous year) while 12 were still under examination, according to the report.

This may point to the beginning of a rising role of whistleblowers in aiding stock-market policing amid the rapid expansion in capital markets in recent years.

The stock exchanges have added over 180 million investors and hundreds of companies since FY19, the last year before the establishment of the whistleblower mechanism.

The regulator added more than 300 employees since FY19 and invested in advanced technology to keep up with increased demands.

“This could possibly be a sign of increasing confidence in the reporting mechanism by potential whistleblowers with substantive information in hand to report,” noted Rohitashwa Prasad, partner at law firm Dentons Link Legal. More can be done to encourage people to come forward, he said.

According to Prasad, mature markets such as the United States (US) have limited legal delays and avoid a cap on rewards, besides providing more protection against employer retaliation.

The US Securities Exchange Commission (US SEC) announced a $279 million reward (or over ~2,000 crore, based on the prevailing exchange rate) for a tip in May 2023, shows SEC statement disclosures.

Whistleblowers whose employment is affected because of reporting violations to the regulator have stronger safeguards against retaliation, Prasad said.

“Under the Dodd Frank Act, an employee who has reported to the SEC can make a retaliation claim directly in a federal court,” he said. The SEC website tells whistleblowers facing retaliation that “you may be able to sue your employer in federal court and seek double back pay (with interest), reinstatement, reasonable attorneys’ fees, and reimbursement for certain costs in connection with the litigation”.

The Sebi regulation notes that informants facing retaliation from employers can approach competent courts or tribunals for relief. It also adds that employers found to be in violation may be liable for regulatory action, but adds that “nothing in these regulations will require the Board to direct reinstatement or compensation by an employer”.

Sumit Agrawal, founder, Regstreet Law Advisors and former Sebi officer, noted that there was limited publicly available information on the outcomes of the OIP mechanism. It can be difficult to objectively evaluate the effectiveness of the initiative without granular information on the number of informants rewarded, the number of tipoffs that resulted in investigations or enforcement proceedings, and the eventual outcomes of such proceedings, Agrawal said.

A request under the Right to Information (RTI) Act that Business Standard filed separately also did not result in additional information.

The scope of violations covered by the informant mechanism can also be expanded, according to Agrawal.

“They should consider a mechanism covering all serious security-market violations. The mechanism could include front-running, fraudulent or manipulative conduct, material disclosure violations, falsifying accounts and serious intermediary misconduct. There is no clear policy reason for an incentivised informant mechanism to remain restricted to insider trading,” Agrawal said. An email sent to the regulator did not receive a reply.

item.title: Flipkart deal helps Netflix log record quarterly subscriber gains in India
item.description: Netflix reported record quarterly paid subscriber additions in India and 18 per cent revenue growth in Q3 2026, aided by its transaction-based loyalty partnership with Flipkart ...
item.dc:creator: Peerzada Abrar
item.content:encoded: Flipkart’s partnership with Netflix helped the streaming platform record its highest-ever quarterly paid subscriber additions in India in the July-September quarter, with the company also reporting 18 per cent year-on-year revenue growth in the country. Netflix disclosed the performance in its Q3 2026 shareholder letter, highlighting the results from its first transaction-based loyalty bundle with Flipkart. Announced on July 31, 2026, the partnership allows eligible Flipkart Plus members to earn a 30-day Netflix Mobile subscription every month by completing four qualifying orders of ₹299 or more each. The benefit is available on eligible purchases across Flipkart, Flipkart Grocery and Flipkart Minutes. The model links everyday shopping to entertainment access, allowing customers to unlock a streaming subscription through their transactions rather than paying separately for the qualifying month’s plan. The subscription benefit can be earned again each month by meeting the order requirement. “With our first transaction-based loyalty bundle with Flipkart, we achieved our largest quarter ever of paid net additions in India and grew Q3 revenue in India around 18 per cent year over year on a F/X neutral basis,” Netflix said in its shareholder letter. The partnership brings together Flipkart’s e-commerce, grocery and quick-commerce platforms with Netflix’s streaming service. This is creating a transaction-led route to customer acquisition for the entertainment platform while offering an additional benefit to shoppers. For Flipkart, the arrangement expands the utility of its loyalty programme by connecting shopping frequency with access to a global streaming service. The model also creates an incentive for eligible customers to consolidate more of their monthly purchases on its platforms. Netflix did not disclose the number of subscribers added through the partnership or quantify its contribution to the company’s overall subscriber additions and revenue growth. The India performance comes amid competition among streaming platforms to expand paid subscriptions through local content, pricing strategies and distribution partnerships.
